title: Effective Study Skills
summary: Evidence-based methods for planning, revising, remembering and sitting exams, from secondary school to university.

body.p: A timetable only works if every slot names a task you can finish and check. 'Study Biology' is vague and easy to skip. 'Biology: answer ten past questions on cell division, mark them, list the mistakes' is a task with a clear end. Planning also protects you from the common habit of spending most of your time on the subjects you already enjoy.

steps: List every subject with its exam or test date.
Rate each subject as strong, medium or weak using your last test or mock marks, not your feelings.
Give weak subjects and early exam dates the most sessions.
Make each session 40 to 50 minutes, followed by a break of 10 minutes away from your phone.
Leave at least one half day free for rest, and one slot for catching up on what you missed.
Every Sunday, look back at what you finished and adjust the next week.

body.p: Amina is preparing for school-leaving exams (WAEC, KCSE or A-Levels would all work the same way). Her subjects are Mathematics, English, Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Economics. Her mock marks show Mathematics is weakest, Chemistry and Physics are medium, and the rest are stronger. She has two sessions on weekday evenings after school and two on Saturday morning, so 12 sessions per week. She gives Mathematics 3, Chemistry 2, Physics 2, Biology 2, Economics 2 and English 1.

body.code:
Mon 5:00-5:45  Maths: 10 algebra questions, mark, fix errors
Mon 6:00-6:45  English: one summary paragraph, compare with model
Tue 5:00-5:45  Chemistry: mole calculations from memory, then check
Tue 6:00-6:45  Biology: draw and label the heart without notes
Wed 5:00-5:45  Maths: past paper section A, timed
Wed 6:00-6:45  Economics: explain demand and supply shifts aloud
Thu 5:00-5:45  Physics: 8 mechanics questions
Thu 6:00-6:45  Chemistry: past questions on acids and bases
Fri 5:00-5:45  Maths: redo last week's errors
Fri 6:00-6:45  Biology: self-quiz on cell division
Sat 8:00-9:30  Physics: electricity problems, then review
Sat 10:00-11:30 Economics: one past essay plan, timed

body.tip: Plan fewer hours than you think you have. A plan you complete at 80 percent builds confidence; an overloaded plan you abandon on Wednesday teaches you nothing.

body.p: Retrieval practice means pulling information out of your memory instead of putting it in again. Research on learning has repeatedly found that trying to recall material strengthens memory more than re-reading it does. Re-reading feels productive because the text looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the answer in an exam hall.

list: Close the book and write everything you remember about a topic, then check what you missed.
Use flashcards with a question on one side and the answer on the other, and say the answer before you flip.
Answer past exam questions under realistic conditions, then mark them with the mark scheme.
Explain the topic aloud to a friend or an imaginary class without notes.
Draw diagrams, such as the water cycle or a circuit, from memory.

body.p: Kofi has read a chapter on acids and bases. Instead of reading it again, he closes the book and writes down the definition of an acid, three properties, the pH scale range and one neutralisation equation. He then opens the book, circles what he got wrong or forgot, and writes only those items on flashcards. Tomorrow he will try the flashcards first. The mistakes are useful: they show exactly where the gaps are.

Retrieval will feel harder than re-reading and you will make errors. That difficulty is part of why it works, so do not take mistakes as a sign that you are failing. Do check your answers quickly, because practising a wrong answer can fix it in your mind.

body.tip: Turn headings in your notes into questions. 'Causes of inflation' becomes 'List and explain three causes of inflation', and you answer it from memory.

lessons.title: Spacing your revision and mixing topics

body.p: Spaced practice means returning to material several times, with gaps between sessions, instead of covering it once in a long block. Cramming can help you pass a test tomorrow, but the information fades quickly. Revisiting a topic after a day, then a few days, then a week or two makes you work to remember it, and that effort strengthens the memory.

There is no single perfect interval, but a practical pattern is to review new material the next day, then after about three days, then after a week, then after two to three weeks, always by testing yourself. If a topic feels shaky, bring the next review forward. If it feels easy, push it back.

body.code:
Mon: learn photosynthesis
Tue: quick self-test (10 min)
Fri: self-test and fix gaps
Fri next week: past-exam questions on it
Two weeks later: mixed test with other Biology topics

body.p: Interleaving means mixing different topics or problem types within one session instead of practising one type many times in a row. In Mathematics, a blocked session might be 20 questions on quadratic equations. An interleaved session mixes quadratics, simultaneous equations, ratios and percentages. It feels harder and your accuracy during the session may be lower, but it trains you to decide which method a question needs, which is exactly what an exam asks. Use blocked practice to learn a new method for the first time, then interleave once you know it.

body.tip: Put the date of each review in your timetable when you first learn a topic. If it is not scheduled, it usually does not happen.

body.p: Many students highlight or copy whole paragraphs and then feel they have studied. Highlighting by itself requires little thinking, and long copied notes are rarely reread. Good notes are short, in your own words, and designed to be used for testing yourself later.

body.h: Reading a textbook or lecture handout

steps: Before reading, skim the headings, diagrams and summary to see the structure.
Turn each heading into a question you expect the text to answer.
Read one section, then look away and say or write the answer in your own words.
Note only key terms, rules, causes and examples. Leave out sentences you could look up easily.
Finish by writing three questions that could appear in an exam.

body.h: Before and after: notes on inflation

body.p: Before: three sentences copied from the textbook defining inflation, with the whole paragraph highlighted in yellow. After: a two-column page. The left column holds questions such as 'What is inflation?' and 'Name two causes.' The right column holds short answers: 'A sustained rise in the general price level, so a given amount of money buys less' and 'Demand-pull, cost-push.' Covering the right column turns the page into a self-test.

In a lecture hall, you do not need to write everything the lecturer says. Capture the structure and the examples, leave gaps where you missed something, and fill them in within 24 hours from the slides or a classmate. Reviewing notes soon after class helps you spot confusion while you can still ask about it.

body.tip: If you cannot explain a note without looking at it, you do not yet understand it. Mark it and ask your teacher or lecturer.

lessons.title: Focus, sleep and looking after yourself

body.p: Memory and concentration depend on your body. Sleep is not wasted time before an exam: during sleep your brain consolidates what you learned, and tiredness reduces attention, reasoning and mood the next day. Staying up all night to cram usually costs more than it gains.

list: Keep a regular sleep time most nights, especially in exam weeks.
Eat regular meals and drink water. Hunger and dehydration make it harder to concentrate.
Move for a few minutes in your breaks, for example a short walk.
Study in the same quiet place when you can, with a clear desk.
Take breaks away from screens so that the break is real rest.

body.p: Every notification pulls attention away, and getting back into a hard problem takes time. Put your phone in another room or switch it to silent and out of reach during sessions. If you use your phone for study apps or a timer, turn off notifications from messaging and social media. Tell family or housemates your study times if that helps.

body.h: When it feels like too much

body.p: Some stress before exams is normal. Breaking work into small tasks, keeping your timetable realistic and talking to a friend or teacher can help. If worry stops you sleeping, eating or functioning for a long period, speak to a counsellor, a doctor or your school or university support service. This course cannot give medical advice.

body.tip: On the night before an exam, do a light review of key points, prepare your pens, ID and route, and go to bed at your normal time.

lessons.title: Exam technique and learning from mistakes

body.p: Knowing the content is only part of an exam. Technique means reading questions carefully, using time sensibly and giving the examiner what the question asks for. Practise it with timed past papers, because speed and accuracy under time pressure are skills of their own.

steps: Read all instructions and check how many questions you must answer.
Estimate time from marks. In a 120-minute paper worth 100 marks, a 10-mark question deserves about 12 minutes, including planning.
Underline the command word. 'State' wants a short fact, 'explain' wants a reason, 'compare' wants similarities and differences, 'evaluate' wants a judgement supported by evidence.
Start with questions you can answer, but do not leave a question blank. Partial working in Mathematics and Science can earn marks.
Leave five minutes to check numbers, units and that you answered every part.

body.p: After a timed paper, mark it with the mark scheme and write an error log. For each lost mark, record the question, the reason (did not know, misread the question, careless mistake, ran out of time) and the fix. Then retest those items a week later. If most errors are carelessness, slow down and check; if they are gaps in knowledge, return to retrieval practice on those topics.

body.code:
Q7 Physics  | wrong unit (cm instead of m) | careless | underline units, check at the end
Q12 Biology | confused osmosis and diffusion | gap | flashcard, retest Friday

body.tip: Never spend ten minutes stuck on a 2-mark question. Mark it, move on and come back if time allows.

quiz.q: Mock results show Chika is weak in Mathematics, medium in Physics and strong in English. She has 12 weekly study sessions. Which allocation best follows the planning advice?
options: Four sessions each for the three subjects, so that no subject is favoured over the others
Mostly English, because it is where she scores best
Mathematics 6, Physics 4, English 2, with English kept in the plan
Only Mathematics until she scores full marks

quiz.q: After reading a chapter on the heart, which action is the best use of the next 15 minutes?
options: Close the book and draw and label the heart from memory, then check it
Read the whole chapter again from the start, slowly, so that every detail is fresh in your mind
Highlight the key terms in a second colour
Copy the chapter summary neatly

quiz.q: A student says, 'I reread my notes five times and everything looked familiar, so I know it.' What is the main problem with this reasoning?
options: Five rereads is too few
Familiarity from rereading can be mistaken for being able to recall the answer
Notes should never be read at all
Familiarity is a reliable sign of mastery

quiz.q: You learn a new topic on Monday. Which review plan best uses spaced practice?
options: Study it for four hours on Monday and then stop
Test yourself on Tuesday, again later in the week, then after a week or more
Review it only the night before the exam
Reread it every hour on Monday

quiz.q: Which session is an example of interleaving?
options: Thirty questions on quadratic equations, one after another, until the method feels automatic
Reading one Biology chapter three times
One practice set mixing quadratics, ratios, percentages and simultaneous equations
Studying Chemistry on Monday and Physics on Tuesday

quiz.q: Interleaved practice feels harder and your scores in the session are lower than with blocked practice. What should you conclude?
options: This difficulty is expected and the method is still useful for later exam performance
You should return to blocked practice permanently
You are not suited to Mathematics
The method has failed

quiz.q: Which set of notes is best prepared for later self-testing?
options: Whole paragraphs copied from the textbook in neat handwriting, with the key sentences highlighted in yellow
A photograph of the textbook page
A typed copy of the lecturer's slides
Questions in one column and short own-word answers in another, which can be covered

quiz.q: A 90-minute paper has 90 marks. A 15-mark question is worth how much time, including planning?
options: About 5 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 30 minutes
As long as it takes, since the other questions are easier

quiz.q: A question begins with 'Evaluate'. What should your answer contain?
options: A one-line definition
A list of facts with no conclusion
A judgement supported by evidence and balanced points
A copy of the question rewritten in your own words, followed by a long list of related facts

quiz.q: After a practice paper, Ife notices most lost marks were from wrong units and misread questions. What is the best response?
options: Add a checking routine such as underlining units and rereading the question, and log the errors
Memorise the whole syllabus again from the beginning, since the marks were clearly lost through poor knowledge
Ignore it because they were only small mistakes
Stop doing timed papers

quiz.q: It is the night before an important exam and you have studied steadily for weeks. Which plan is most sensible?
options: Study until 4 a.m. so that you can cover every topic one more time before the exam begins
Skip dinner to save time for revision
Study new topics you have not covered
Do a light review of key points, prepare your materials and sleep at your usual time

quiz.q: You are on a hard Mathematics question worth 2 marks and have spent several minutes without progress. What should you do?
options: Keep going until you solve it
Mark it, move on to other questions and return if time remains
Leave the paper early
Guess and never look at it again
